measures: What a school's catalog offers. Not what a graduate leaves with, and not what is required — see limitations.
limitations: OFFERED, NOT REQUIRED. harvest.py reads course descriptions, not degree requirement sheets, so nothing here can distinguish a required professional-practice course from an elective nobody takes. The Venture axis in particular means much less without it. Either harvest program pages, or state plainly that edition one measures offering.

Denominator is the whole catalog, not the art catalog. A large public university dilutes: 40 art-business courses among 6,000 total scores lower than 10 among 400. Normalizing by CIP-50-relevant courses rather than all courses is unresolved.
Thresholds below are placeholders. They must be set from the observed distribution once enough schools are scored, and the rule used must be published.

technology.name: Art Technology Adoption
technology.question: Does this course teach making with computational or emerging tools — AI, code, generative systems, immersive media, digital fabrication — or teach a specific software or hardware toolset for creative work?
includes: AI readiness, generative tools, machine learning as material
creative coding, computational and algorithmic making
immersive, XR, game engines, virtual production
digital fabrication, CNC, 3D printing, physical computing
named software or hardware toolsets taught for creative work
excludes: computer science, data science or engineering outside an art or design subject
art history or theory that discusses technology without making
technical trade production where the tool is the trade — audio plugin development, architectural lighting

venture.name: Art Venture and Enterprise
venture.question: Does this course teach building an enterprise around your own creative work — business formation, revenue, pricing, funding, self-employment, running a studio as a business? The test is whether the student is taught to build something of their own, not to operate inside someone else's apparatus.
includes: business formation, business models, startup and studio-as-business
pricing, revenue, contracts and negotiation for one's own work
self-employment, freelancing as an enterprise, financial management for artists
grant writing and fundraising to finance one's own practice
intellectual property, licensing and royalties as revenue
excludes: portfolio, interviewing, resume, submission preparation — PRACTICE
gallery submission, residency application, competition entry — PRACTICE
professional licensure, accreditation, internship placement — PRACTICE
SENIOR STUDIO, capstone, degree project, thesis studio — these are STUDIO, even when the description mentions professional context
medium and technique courses that mention industry or clients in passing — IMAGE DESIGN, ILLUSTRATING FOR SURFACE & PATTERN DESIGN are illustration courses
entrepreneurship taught outside art and design — The Entrepreneurial Bioengineer
accounting, finance or management taught for business students
arts administration training administrators rather than artists

practice.name: Professional Practice and Readiness
practice.question: Does this course teach operating inside an existing professional apparatus — portfolio, interviewing, submission, licensure, and the craft of curating, exhibiting or publishing? This is the control axis: it is what nearly every program already teaches, and it is what venture is usually mistaken for.
includes: portfolio development, portfolio review, artist statement as submission material
interviewing, job search, career preparation for employment
gallery, residency, competition and grant SUBMISSION mechanics
how to curate, how to exhibit, how to publish — the craft of these
professional licensure, accreditation, industry-standard practice
excludes: building an enterprise around one's own work — VENTURE
reaching people directly with one's own work — AUDIENCE
SENIOR STUDIO, senior seminar in a medium, capstone, degree project, thesis studio — these are STUDIO. Senior Photography and Senior Sculpture are studio courses, not professional readiness
studio and technique courses that mention portfolio or industry in passing — Functional Design for High-Performance Eyewear is a design course
art history and curatorial theory — that is HISTORY unless the course teaches the craft of curating as professional work

self.name: Creative Self-Development Science
self.question: Does this course teach creative process, creative development, or the person making the work as its subject — how ideas form, how a practice is navigated and sustained, how a creative life is designed?
includes: creativity science, creative cognition, psychology of creativity
creative process and ideation taught as transferable method
personal and artistic development, artistic identity and voice
life design for artists, sustaining a practice, artist wellbeing and burnout
contemplative, somatic and embodiment practice taught as creative method
critique taught explicitly as a method
excludes: ANY studio, media or technique course where making is the content

A studio course does not become a Self course by saying it develops expression, confidence, creativity or personal voice. Those phrases describe an OUTCOME of making and appear in studio boilerplate across the corpus. CalArts AART 220 'Writing' declares itself part of the Studio Series, counts toward the studio requirement, and uses language as its medium — it is a studio course. If the description says studio, counts toward a studio requirement, or names a medium the student will work in, it is excluded however the outcomes are worded.
thesis or capstone whose subject is the student's own project — BUT a seminar that explicitly teaches how ideas form or how a practice is navigated DOES count
courses that merely use the words creative or creativity in describing studio work
performance and somatic training taught for performance rather than as creative method

audience.name: Audience and Distribution
audience.question: Does this course teach connecting your own work to people — marketing, sales, social media, storytelling for reach, self-distribution, building a following? The vehicle does not matter; the subject is reaching an audience directly.
includes: marketing and sales for artists and designers
social media, online presence, content and platform strategy
storytelling and narrative deployed to reach an audience
self-publishing, self-distribution, direct-to-audience channels
audience development, community and public engagement with one's own work
curating, exhibiting or publishing WHEN the subject is connecting work to people
excludes: HOW TO curate, exhibit or publish as a craft — that is PRACTICE
art history, survey and museum studies
rhetoric and composition treating audience as a writing concept
research methods mentioning published research or documentation of findings
statistics and science using distribution in its technical sense

prefilter.note: Stage one is tuned for RECALL, not precision. Over-matching is fine and expected; stage two removes the false positives. Under-matching is invisible and unrecoverable, so err wide.

classifier.note: Temperature 0 and a cached result per course-text hash, so a rerun reproduces exactly. Every classification is logged with the model and rubric version.
classifier.instruction:
For each course decide which categories, if any, it belongs to. The default is none: most courses in a university catalog belong to no category, and an empty array is the expected answer.

Apply one test per category. Would a student describing this course to a friend name the category's subject as what the course is ABOUT? If the category's subject is instead the medium, the tool, the setting, or one component of a studio course, the answer is no.

Judge what the course teaches, not what words appear in it. A ceramics course that develops the student's creative process is a ceramics course. A painting course that mentions selling work is a painting course. A statistics course using the word distribution is a statistics course. When a course is genuinely borderline, exclude it — a missing true positive costs one course; a false positive is published as evidence.

The exclusions describe subjects, not course types. Never reject a course because its title contains thesis, seminar, capstone, studio or workshop; reject it because what it teaches is the student's own project, a medium, or a technique. A course named 'Thesis Seminar: Navigating the Creative Process' teaches creative process and counts.

TWO CATEGORIES ARE MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE. Never assign both venture and practice to the same course. They are one distinction, not two categories: what is the student taught to depend on? Venture is building something of their own — business formation, revenue, pricing, funding, self-employment, running a studio as an enterprise. Practice is operating inside an apparatus someone else built — portfolio, interviewing, submission, licensure, internship, the craft of curating or exhibiting as a job.

When a course teaches both, choose the larger part. When it is genuinely balanced, choose practice. A course called 'Professional Practice' that includes a unit on pricing is practice. 'What Next? Making a Living as an Artist' is practice unless the course is predominantly about building a business. Choosing practice on a tie is deliberate: it is the more common and less flattering reading, and this index must not overstate how much enterprise training exists.
classifier.model_note:
The model is part of the instrument. Sonnet 4.6 and Haiku 4.5 read this rubric differently enough to change every axis: on five schools under an identical rubric file, Haiku returned 1.43x more matches overall, 7.8x more Self at RISD, and put studio courses back into Self at CalArts — the failure v0.3 was written to fix. Every adjudication in this project's history ran on Sonnet. Changing the model is a version bump, never a flag.

claude-sonnet-4-6 is already the most specific identifier: from the 4.6 generation onward model IDs are dateless AND pinned to a single fixed snapshot, so there is no dated form to prefer. Record it verbatim in the methodology.

matching.rule: Each term is compiled with word boundaries. A trailing * means prefix match: 'negotiat*' matches negotiate, negotiating, negotiation.
matching.why: v0.1 stripped whitespace off every term before escaping it, so ' ai ' compiled to a bare substring 'ai' and matched painting, detail, available, maintain, chair. 'unity' matched community. 'tax' matched taxonomy. 'contract' matched contraction. On an art catalog the technology axis matched close to everything, which makes the shortlist rate useless as a diagnostic.

flagged_for_author.note: Not changed in v0.2 — each is an editorial call, not a mechanical repair. Run lexprobe.py and decide from the counts and samples.

probably_dead_phrases.why: No registrar writes these. A dead term cannot lower a score, only fail to raise one — so the Self axis scoring near zero would be manufactured by the lexicon rather than found in the world. That is the index's strongest sentence and it must not be an artifact.

high_carry_boilerplate.why: Catalog boilerplate ('prepares students for careers in...', 'satisfies the general education distribution requirement', 'unity of composition'). Stage two rejects them correctly, but if one term carries >40% of an axis's shortlist the axis is measuring that word. Check carry% in lexprobe before spending on stage two.

v0_4_note.hypothesis: Sonnet was not over-rejecting Self; it was executing a badly written exclude literally. Haiku ignored the same exclude, which masked the error.
v0_4_note.test: Re-run RISD alone against v0.4 on Sonnet. If ARCH 2196 returns as a Self match and the drawing and sketchbook studios stay out, the hypothesis holds and Sonnet is the better instrument precisely because it follows the rubric.
v0_4_note.if_it_holds: RISD Self = 1. One course teaching creative process as method at one of the strongest art schools in the country is the finding, not a miss.

structure.note: Technology and audience are sub-aspects of venture, not peers of it: both are capacities a venture needs. So the five axes are NOT orthogonal and MUST NOT be averaged into a composite — doing so double-counts venture. Report five separate percentages. A course may carry more than one axis (sales for artists is venture and audience), so per-school percentages may sum above 100% and that is correct.

denominator.rule: n_matched / n_art_courses — the school's own art unit, never the whole catalog
denominator.why: The question is what fraction of an art unit's offerings sit on each axis. Whole-catalog share answers a different question nobody asked. A 400-course art unit at 60% venture beats a 400-course art unit at 30% venture regardless of what else the parent university offers.
denominator.known_limitation: The art-subject set moves a median 10.6% between classifier models. This is stated, and reduced by improving the subject classifier — not a reason to use a denominator that answers a different question.

subsets.venture.entrepreneurship_explicit: flag venture matches whose TITLE contains entrepreneur/entrepreneurship, reported as a named subset count alongside the venture percentage

axis_exclusivity.rule: VENTURE and PRACTICE are mutually exclusive. A course carries at most one.
axis_exclusivity.why: They are a split of one thing — what the student is taught to depend on. Allowing both double-counted roughly 30% of venture matches in v0.5: RISD FD 2582, GRAD 144G, ILLUS 4012; MassArt EDID 230, MPFV 327; Temple ART 4096, ART 4097.
axis_exclusivity.tiebreak: If a course teaches both — a professional-practice course with a business module — assign VENTURE only when building one's own enterprise is the course's larger part. Otherwise PRACTICE. When genuinely balanced, choose PRACTICE: it is the more common and less flattering reading, and the index should not overstate venture.
axis_exclusivity.still_multi_label: Other pairs may co-occur. Sales for artists is VENTURE and AUDIENCE. Technology and audience remain sub-aspects of venture.
axis_exclusivity.enforcement: The rule now lives in classifier.instruction, which build_prompt actually reads. In v0.6 it lived only in this block, which nothing consumes — the model never saw it, and 2-6 courses per school came back with both. Belt and braces: score.py should ALSO drop venture whenever practice is present on the same course, after classification. Deterministic, cannot drift, and it makes the tiebreak a property of the code rather than a hope about the model.

composition.purpose: A second, separate classification: every course in the art unit gets exactly ONE primary bucket. Exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so the buckets sum to 100% of the art unit. This answers a dean's first question — what is my curriculum actually made of — which the five axes cannot, because they only measure the parts the index cares about and overlap by design. Report composition as a pie; report axes as five percentages alongside it.
composition.question: What is this course primarily? Choose exactly one bucket. Judge what the course teaches, not what words appear in it. When a course could sit in two, choose the one a student would name if asked what the class was about.

buckets.studio: Making in a medium or technique — painting, ceramics, typography, animation, photography, industrial design studio. The core of an art curriculum.
buckets.history_theory: Art and design history, visual culture, theory, criticism, curatorial and museum studies as scholarship.
buckets.liberal_arts: Writing, literature, philosophy, science, mathematics, language, social science — non-art coursework offered inside or required by the art unit.
buckets.practice: Professional readiness: portfolio, interviewing, submission, licensure, internship preparation, the craft of curating or exhibiting as a job.
buckets.venture: Building an enterprise around one's own work: business formation, revenue, pricing, funding, self-employment, studio as a business.
buckets.technology: Computational and emerging tools, and named software or hardware toolsets taught for creative work.
buckets.self: Creative process, creativity science, artistic development, life design for artists, sustaining a practice.
buckets.audience: Marketing, sales, social media, storytelling for reach, self-distribution, audience development for one's own work.
buckets.capstone: Thesis, degree project, senior studio, final project, graduate seminar tied to the student's own body of work.
buckets.independent: Independent study, directed study, special topics with no fixed content, internship placements, administrative registration shells.
buckets.pedagogy: Art education and teacher preparation — training teachers rather than artists.
buckets.other: Anything that fits none of the above. If this bucket exceeds ~5% of a school, the taxonomy is wrong and should be revised rather than forced.

notes: CalArts carries 2,603 administrative shells — Independent Study, Internship and Thesis replicated once per department per level — which is 38% of its catalog. The independent bucket makes that visible instead of letting it silently dilute every percentage.
capstone is separated from studio deliberately. A senior thesis studio is not the same curricular object as a sophomore painting course, and deans reason about them differently.

The five axis percentages and the composition percentages will not agree exactly. Axes allow overlap and are measured against matched courses; composition is one-per-course and exhaustive. Both are reported, and the difference is stated rather than reconciled.
composition.scope: Runs over EVERY course in the school's art-subject set — no prefilter. The prefilter exists to keep cost down across 500k records; an art unit is a few hundred to a few thousand courses, so classifying all of them removes the prefilter as a source of error entirely for the dean-facing product.
composition.pedagogy_after_the_exclusion: The pedagogy bucket already exists and is not missing — 507 courses, 0.97% of the corpus. But excluding art-education PREFIXES from the art unit changes what it counts, and the methodology must say so: pedagogy now means ART EDUCATION TAUGHT INSIDE AN ART DEPARTMENT, not all art education at that institution. Temple's ARTE sequence is in; Florida State's ARE prefix is not. That is the right denominator — the art unit is what art students are offered — but a reader comparing our pedagogy share to a school's art-education enrolment would otherwise be comparing two different things.

subject_scope.in_scope: CIP 50.01 visual and performing arts general, 50.02 crafts, 50.04 design and applied arts (including 50.0402 commercial and advertising art), 50.06 film/video/photographic arts, 50.07 fine and studio arts, 50.13 community, environmental and socially-engaged art — the same selection that built the roster. Every other CIP 50 family, including 50.05 drama and theatre and 50.10 arts management, is out.
excluded_families: performing arts: music, theatre, dance — including technique, partnering, audition and repertory prefixes
building and industrial trades (CIP 46, 47, 48) — carpentry, electrical, HVAC, plumbing, welding
agriculture and natural resources (01, 03), including horticulture
communication and journalism (CIP 09) — advertising as communication (09.0903), public relations, media studies, journalism

NOTE, and this is the case the test exists for: advertising DESIGN is CIP 50.0402 Commercial and Advertising Art, which is IN SCOPE. SCAD's ADVE — 'Typography for Advertising Designers', 'Art Direction and Typography Essentials', 'Advertising Studio I: Creative Strategies' — is a design department and stays in. SMU's ADV, Virginia Tech's ADV and Tennessee's ADVT — 'Marketing Principles of Advertising', 'Account Planning and Media Buying', 'Advertising Media Strategy' — are communication departments and stay out. Decide by what the courses teach. Never by the prefix name.
education and teacher preparation, except where the courses are studio art courses

ARCHITECTURE, LANDSCAPE ARCHITECTURE, URBAN AND REGIONAL PLANNING, HISTORIC PRESERVATION — programmes that design BUILDINGS, SITES, LANDSCAPES AND URBAN FORM FOR CONSTRUCTION. Judge by what the prefix's courses design, never by the word design.

THIS IS NOT AN EXCLUSION OF DESIGN. Graphic, communication, visual, industrial, product, interior, interaction, user-experience, service, game, fashion and textile design are CIP 50.04 and are IN. So are design studies, design management and design research. If a prefix teaches designing OBJECTS, IMAGES, INTERFACES, GARMENTS OR EXPERIENCES rather than buildings and sites, it is IN — Advanced Design Studies, UX Research, Design Management and Preservation Design read as design and belong to the art unit.

The test in one line: does the prefix train people to put up structures, or to make things?
subject_scope.protected: These stay IN even though a neighbouring family is excluded, because they are CIP 50: communication design, graphic design and visual communication (50.04); scientific, technical and medical illustration (50.04); industrial, interior and fashion design (50.04); film, video and photography (50.06). The test is what the prefix's courses teach, not what the prefix is named. A prefix whose courses are design or image-making is in; a prefix whose courses are journalism, public relations, advertising management or media theory is out, even if it sits administratively in a design school.
subject_scope.excluded_delivery: Continuing education, extension, pre-college, summer intensive and non-credit prefixes are excluded whatever their subject. The index measures what a degree programme teaches its degree students. CalArts XYTH 805 'Discover Studio Art - 1 Week' entered Self through this gap. Report the count excluded per school so the decision is visible and reversible.
subject_scope.not_subjects: Campus, location and administrative codes are not subject codes and are excluded by definition — the taxonomy classifies disciplines, and a location cannot be art or not-art. Temple's TUJ (Japan campus) is excluded on this ground rather than on any rule about where a student can enrol. TYLE (Tyler School of Art) stays in; it names a discipline unit.
subject_scope.positive_rule: Include a prefix only when most of its sample titles are art and design courses.
subject_scope.sampling: A prefix is judged from a sample of its course titles. Sample randomly, not the first N, and use enough titles that a large prefix is not decided on a thin slice. Emerson's VM — 150 courses, its visual and media arts department, CIP 50.06 work — was excluded entirely on five sampled titles that all happened to be media-studies courses. Record the sample size on the record so a reader knows what the judgement rested on.
subject_scope.scope_change_implementation: A scope change must never be made by editing the subject prompt. Editing it re-keys every prefix in the corpus and re-rolls every verdict — the Loyola Marymount instability at corpus scale, on the eve of publication. Ask a narrow follow-up question of prefixes currently judged 'art' only, cached per prefix, so no existing verdict can move.

publication.why:
TECHNOLOGY AND PRACTICE RANK. VENTURE, SELF AND AUDIENCE ARE CENSUSES — named courses with source URLs and a count per school, no rank.

This reverses v0.28, which made all five rank on Brink's instruction, and the reason is evidence that did not exist then: measured against a 158-course oracle, the venture classifier is 16% wrong under the best-tested wording and 11% of the population is undecidable by the person who knows the corpus best. A ranking asserts an order between schools; a census asserts that these named courses exist and these named schools have none. The second claim survives a 16% error rate with every course listed and checkable. The first does not.

Self and audience were already censuses on their own numbers — 10 and 14 schools clearing the three-course floor out of 144. Venture clears 23, but clearing a floor is not the same as being measurable to the precision a rank implies.

State the census population on every surface: how many schools have three or more, how many have none, and the named courses behind both.
publication.minimum_count_rule:
A school takes a position on an axis only when it carries at least three matched courses there. Below three it is listed with its count, in grey, with no rank — and it is NOT ranked among the schools that do. One course in a 94-course art unit is 1.06% and would have placed fourth in the country; that is a denominator artefact, not a finding.

THIS RULE ALREADY DECIDES THE TWO CASES THE MAKER RULE RAISED, and neither should ever have produced a rank. Western Carolina gains two venture courses in a 152-course art unit: two is below three, so it takes no venture position and the reported move to 6th does not exist. Oklahoma State loses its single venture course: one is below three, so its reported fall from 37th to 97th does not exist either. If a ranking produced those numbers, the floor is not being applied where ranks are computed — check that before anything else, because every sparse-axis rank in the index has the same exposure.
publication.always_show_count: Every published percentage carries its numerator and denominator — '5 of 182 courses (2.75%)' — on every axis, in every surface, including any sortable table. The count is what makes a share interpretable and it is the first thing a dean checks.
publication.denominator_disclosure:
Both denominators are computed and the ranking uses the art unit. Publish these numbers, measured on the current corpus, rather than a correlation alone.

Spearman between whole-catalogue and art-unit rank: technology +0.734, practice +0.475, venture +0.447, self +0.436, audience +0.396. Mean +0.498.

BOTH DENOMINATORS CARRY ARTEFACTS AND THEY POINT OPPOSITE WAYS. Whole-catalogue inflates art colleges, whose catalogues are ~74% art against a university's ~6%. The art unit amplifies single courses at small units. Neither is neutral, and the two named movers show the direction: George Mason, 5% art share, moves 93.6 to 36.2; FIT, 56% art share, moves 8.6 to 54.2. Low-art-share schools rise under the art unit and high-art-share schools fall, which is the exact inverse of the whole-catalogue bias.

THE MEAN HAS FALLEN AS THE CORPUS GREW — +0.611 at n=108, +0.517 at n=132, +0.498 now. The denominator has become MORE load-bearing, not less, as the art unit got cleaner. Venture sits at +0.447: roughly half the rank order on the axis carrying the central claim is a consequence of how the art unit is defined.

SO: lead with count and share, which are a school's own numbers over its own courses and move only when its own catalogue does. Treat rank as derived and dated — true as of a stated corpus, moving when anyone's denominator moves, not only that school's. This is the reason the index prints a count beside every percentage, and the methodology should say so rather than leave a reader to infer it.
census_claims: In 61 of 123 American art and design units we could not identify a single course in building a creative enterprise. At 58 of those, entrepreneurship is taught elsewhere on campus.
Every one of the 123 teaches professional practice.
Eighteen of 123 units offer three or more courses in building a creative enterprise.
publication.tier_and_reporting: The RANKED tier stays as the roster defines it: institutions granting 50 or more in-scope bachelor's and master's degrees a year. That rule is mechanical, published and reproducible by anyone with IPEDS, and it must not acquire an exception keyed to another publication's editorial judgement — a US News carve-out would make our roster partly a derivative of theirs and partly unreproducible. Any in-scope programme that has been harvested is REPORTED with a full scorecard whatever its size, carrying the stated reason 'below the 50-degree ranking tier'. Which programmes get collected first is an editorial priority and may follow visibility; which programmes get ranked is a rule. Keeping those separate is what lets the index say 'we read Stanford's catalog; here is what it teaches' without importing anyone else's ranking into our own.
publication.duplicate_catalogs: Two institutions publishing a byte-identical catalog are one catalog and must be reported once, under the name of the institution that publishes it, with the relationship stated. Bloomfield College of Montclair State and Montclair State share 5,479 identical courses; report as Montclair State, note the merger, and sum their in-scope degrees for the tier test. Counting both inflates the corpus with a school that was never independently measured.
publication.subject_set_stability: A school's art-subject set must not move when its course list grows for unrelated reasons. Loyola Marymount's art unit went 268 to 319 on one added course, because re-keying re-ran the whole-school verdict and it admitted an extra department. For a published index that is a school's number changing between editions with no curricular cause, which is the one thing a provost can prove is wrong. Judge and cache each prefix independently, so adding a course can only affect the prefix it belongs to.
publication.debut_convention: The maker rule can move a school's count across the three-course threshold, and when it does the school appears on an axis where it had no position. That is a debut, not a rise, and the changelog must say so: the prefix admitted, its n, its three ratios, and the count that crossed the floor. A school appearing at 6th looks like a finding and is a population change.
publication.ranked_population:
Every axis publishes its ELIGIBLE POPULATION beside every rank, always: 'NC State, 1st of 23 ranked on venture'. The populations differ enormously — technology 114 of 144, practice 121, venture 23, audience 14, self 10 — and a rank without its population is the single most misreadable number the index produces.

SELF STAYS RANKED, at ten. Ranking ten schools out of 144 is defensible only if the ten are named as ten, and then it is not a league table at all — it is the finding, printed as an ordering. CalArts at 23 courses, SVA at 11, USC at 5 are real differences between real counts. What must never appear is a self rank that implies the other 134 schools are ordered below the ten: they are not ranked, most are at zero, and zero is not a position. The population line for self is the headline for that axis, not a caveat under it.
publication.withheld_counts:
Verdicts withheld for want of a published description are counted and published, and the ART-UNIT figure is the one on the scorecard, with the whole-catalogue figure beside it — the same convention as n_collapsed and the raw counts already on the card.

The card's job is to explain that school's published numbers, and those use the art-unit denominator. A whole-shortlist count includes courses that were never in the numerator, so publishing it alone would overstate the effect on the school's own score. Montclair's 42 is a corpus number; what a Montclair dean needs is how many of their ART-UNIT courses the index could not read.
publication.venture_is_a_census:
VENTURE IS REPORTED AS A CENSUS — named courses with source URLs and a count per school — and carries NO RANK. Self and audience already work this way; venture joins them.

THIS IS NOT THE EDIT FAILING. It is a measurement limit, and the evidence is that the person who knows this corpus best marked 17 of 158 courses as landing either way — 11% that no defensible instruction has to resolve. 'The Business of X' is three different courses: X as an industry (Business of Fashion, of Animation) describes how a sector operates; X as a career (Business Practices for Interior Designers) prepares someone to be hired; X as the student's own medium (The Business of Jewelry) teaches them to run their shop. Fashion is both a medium and an industry and the title cannot tell you which. Nineteen of twenty-three remaining misses have that shape.

A 16% error rate is fatal to a ranking and survivable in a census where every course is listed with its URL and a reader can check each one. Seven wordings were tested at $22.94; each fixed the last failure and reintroduced an earlier one. That pattern is what a resolution limit looks like from the inside, and the honest response is to change what the axis claims rather than to keep tuning past it.

PUBLISH THE 17 AS A NAMED DISPUTED SET, with both readings and the source URL for each. A census that says 'these seventeen could be read either way, here they are' is stronger than one that hides them inside a number, and it is the sentence no competing index can write.

override_policy:
An override may only ever APPLY the rubric's content test where a verdict failed it. It may never contradict the test to reach a preferred answer — that is a hand edit and a hostile reader will find it. Every override is published with its reason and the classifier's own verdict beside it.

Overrides do not scale, and this is a hard limit rather than a preference. Two in 165 schools is a correction; twenty is an undocumented rule. A class only counts as a class once the instrument that found it has been checked. The first consensus scan reported 50 against consensus; most were its own false positives — delivery exclusions counted as dissent, and a film shape that matched any title containing 'film' or 'animation', sweeping in journalism, theatre and communication and reporting them as a class of 13. This policy responds to class size, so a scan that manufactures a class would have fired it on nothing. Verify the finder before acting on the finding.

Before publication, run the consensus scan — every prefix whose verdict disagrees with the corpus consensus for prefixes of its shape — and read it. If it returns a handful, overrides stay. If it returns a class, write the rule instead, because a rule is reproducible by a hostile provost and a list of exceptions is not.

AND THE SAME BAR APPLIES TO RULES. Measure the class before writing the rule, not after. Every scope rule, in either direction, needs a MAJORITY test: most of a prefix's sampled courses must belong, never merely some. An existence test admits a whole department for one course, and it has now done so three times in this project — an exclude rule that removed any prefix mentioning architecture, an include rule that admitted departments for a few film titles, and my arts-business rule that admitted 735 music courses at CalArts.

post_classification_scope.how: Everything in this block is applied as a NARROW CACHED FOLLOW-UP asked of already-judged prefixes, never by editing the subject prompt. The subject prompt must stay byte-identical to v0.10 — editing it re-keys every prefix in the corpus and re-rolls every verdict, which is the Loyola Marymount instability at corpus scale. v0.11 put the architecture rule in excluded_families, which IS rendered into the prompt, and would have done exactly that. The pipeline caught it. This block exists so the mistake cannot recur.

Counted at 49 of 54 comparable departments already; the consensus scan found four judged against that consensus — Georgia Gwinnett FILM, Oberlin CIME, Marist MDIA, North Texas MRTS.

THE BOUNDARY, which is where this rule could do damage: making or studying moving images is in. Journalism and broadcast news, communication and public relations, theatre and acting, and media studies taught as social science are OUT, whatever the word 'film' or 'media' is doing in the title. The corrected consensus scan already vetoes that wording; carry the same vetoes here. Ask only of prefixes currently judged 'out' whose titles carry the film shape, and judge by course content as everywhere else.

NOT ENABLED. Drafted, corrected, and held until a scan shows there is a class to rule on.

WHAT WENT WRONG: I wrote 'does this prefix ALSO carry arts business' — an existence test, not a majority test. Any music department with one Business of Music course passes it. Applied, it admitted 155 prefixes, overwhelmingly music and dance: CalArts MITM brought in 735 music courses (Accelerationism & Music, Bach Studies, Applied Flute, Advanced Studio Oboe), plus Cal Poly MU and DANC, East Carolina MUSC, Kent State MUS, Fordham DANC, Liberty MUSC. The pipeline had already learned this in both directions — an exclude rule that removed any prefix MENTIONING architecture, an include rule that admitted whole departments for a few film titles — and fixed both with a majority test. I wrote a new rule without carrying that lesson across.

THE CORRECTED TEXT, if a scan ever justifies enabling it: a prefix currently judged 'out' is IN only when MOST of its sampled courses are arts business, arts leadership, arts management for practitioners, or arts entrepreneurship. Music, dance and theatre prefixes stay OUT regardless of how many business courses they carry. JMU's ARTE would still pass — all four of its courses are arts business and none is teacher preparation.

BEFORE ENABLING IT: run the scan. Count prefixes currently judged 'out' whose sampled titles are MOSTLY arts business. A handful means overrides, which is what the override policy says and what the consensus scan already found — 12 genuine disagreements corpus-wide. A class means write the rule. I wrote a corpus-wide rule for one school, which is precisely what the policy forbids.

MEASURED, AND IT STAYS HELD. The scan found a class of five prefixes and 34 courses: NC State EMA (15), Oklahoma State AADM (8), Utah Tech ARTM (4), JMU ARTE (4, already overridden), JMU ARTS (3). post_classification_scope.makers_practice_rule:
DOCUMENTATION, NOT AN EXECUTABLE FOLLOW-UP. No _in or _out suffix, deliberately. The maker rule is implemented in code from maker_rule.lexicons; this entry explains it. Keys in this block ending _in or _out are executed by followup_rules(), which reads direction from the suffix — so naming it makers_practice_in would have sent this prose to the model against every out-prefix in the corpus, roughly 18,000 uncached asks returning answers that are not the rule. Skipped and logged exactly as arts_business_under_education_HELD is.

THE MAKER RULE. An additional admission path, applied as a narrow cached follow-up. It admits; it never removes, and it never overrides a family exclusion.

ORDER OF APPLICATION: the family exclusions in subject_scope apply first and absolutely — music, dance, theatre, trades, agriculture, life sciences, communication and journalism, family and consumer sciences, architecture. This rule may only admit a prefix that no family exclusion has already removed. That is why it needs no performing-arts term of its own, and it is why DePaul PAM (Performing Arts Management, artperf 0.88) cannot be admitted by it.

THE TEST, on prefixes currently judged out:
  maker's practice  >= 0.50   share of sampled titles addressing someone MAKING the work — their own practice, their own business, their own career as a maker
  art referent      >= 0.50   share naming art, design, creative or cultural work
  admin_only        <  0.50   share that is administrator training and nothing else

WHY MAKER'S PRACTICE AND NOT BUSINESS SHAPE. My §5 ruling was that the test is WHO THE COURSE IS FOR. Business shape measures vocabulary, which is why Oklahoma State's AADM scores 1.00 while being the purest administrator training in the register. Maker's practice measures address: American AMGT 0.03, George Mason AMGT 0.08, AADM 0.12, Utah Tech ARTM 0.25, against NC State EMA 0.87. The pipeline's version implements my ruling more faithfully than my own wording did, and I am adopting theirs.

ONE THRESHOLD IS INERT AND ONE IS LOAD-BEARING, and v0.24 conflated them. admin_only is inert: no prefix clearing maker's practice >= 0.50 has an admin_only above 0.00, so the admit set is identical from 0.2 to 0.6 and there is nothing to defend there. maker's practice is NOT inert: Western Carolina FPA sits at exactly 0.50 and falls out at 0.51. That threshold is a chosen number and must be published as one. It still does not split the two AMGTs — both are below 0.10 — which was the property the rule was picked for.

admin_only stays in the rule although it currently does no work: it is what makes the rule READ as a test of who the course is for rather than an accident of two terms, and it is the term that will matter first when the corpus grows. Note it is asymmetric — a title naming both administration and practice counts on the practice side, so TCU ARLE reads 0.71 admin but 0.29 admin_only. The measure leans generous toward any programme that puts 'entrepreneurship' in an administration title.

ADMITS TODAY: NC State EMA, Western Carolina FPA. Two prefixes.

unranked_reasons.principle: A published reason a school is held back must be mechanically true of that school. A reason is not a diagnosis. The schools least able to object are the ones this lands on, so the bar is that a dean reading it can verify it.
publishable: art-subject set below the 100-course floor — a count, checkable against the published prefix list
description coverage below the 70% floor — a measured rate
fewer than 50 courses harvested — a count
below the 50-degree ranking tier — an IPEDS figure
unranked_reasons.review_only:
'art share implausibly low; subject classification failed' is a REVIEW TRIGGER, not a publishable reason. It is a heuristic on a ratio, and it misfires at large research universities whose art departments are genuinely small relative to the catalog.

Maryland-College Park is the case. Flagged at 1.5%, it turns out to be a correct classification: every one of its largest prefixes — TLPL, INST, ECON, ENGL, PSYC, COMM, MUSC, HIST, BMGT, ENEE, ANTH, CMSC, JOUR, ARCH, THET — is properly out, and its art unit of 86 courses is simply what a 5,770-course university with a modest art department has. Nothing failed. Publishing 'subject classification failed' would have told a dean something untrue about their own institution, and it is exactly the kind of line a provost corrects in public.

So: when the flag fires, read the prefix list. If the verdicts hold, the published reason is the count floor alone. Keep the label only where classification genuinely failed — Penn State 0 of 51 prefixes, UTSA 0 of 63 across 1,864 courses — and say so in those words.
unranked_reasons.maryland: University of Maryland-College Park: publish as 'art-subject set below the 100-course floor (86 courses)'. Drop the classification-failure clause. Its 86 courses are correct.

implementation.note: Nothing in this block is rendered into any prompt. It describes what the pipeline must do, not what a model is told.
implementation.sampling: Sample a prefix's titles with a deterministic seed per (unitid, prefix) — the pipeline uses sha256(unitid|prefix), in place since V20 and verified to draw identical samples on repeat calls. Use enough titles that a large prefix is not decided on a thin slice. Record the sample size and seed on the record.
implementation.verdict_stability_measured: Settled, and my earlier reading was wrong. Columbia's 49 to 88 was not classifier instability: its course file changed between the two runs, 69 graduate-only courses becoming 126 across three departments, so different prefixes and different samples produced different verdicts correctly. Under a fixed seed the two-run comparison shows 0 of 20 prefixes differing at Columbia, JMU and Yale. Three-way voting would buy nothing and should not be built.

publication_bar: The same corpus classified twice must produce identical art-subject sets. Measured, not assumed: it holds.
rendered_blocks:
Blocks whose text reaches a model, and which therefore change a prompt signature when edited: axes[*].name / question / includes / excludes, classifier.instruction, subject_scope, composition.question and composition.buckets. Everything else — post_classification_scope, implementation, publication, subject_overrides, unranked_reasons, axis_exclusivity, override_policy, status — is read by the pipeline and never rendered.

I have now put a rule in a rendered block three times: axis_exclusivity in v0.6 where build_prompt never read it, architecture in excluded_families in v0.11, and sampling in subject_scope in v0.15. Check this list before editing.

AND A SECOND AXIS OF THE SAME ERROR: a key's NAME can make it executable. In post_classification_scope, a suffix of _in or _out means followup_rules() will run it against the corpus; any other name means it is documentation. Before adding a key here, decide which it is. Placement decides whether text reaches a model; naming decides whether it is executed. I have now been wrong about the first three times and the second once.

AND A BIDIRECTIONAL RULE NEEDS TWO KEYS. followup_rules() reads direction from the suffix, so a rule that both admits and removes cannot live under one name — I first wrote the fashion split as fashion_split_rule, which would have been skipped silently like makers_practice_rule and done nothing at all. It is now fashion_design_in and fashion_merchandising_out, one decision under two keys, cross-referenced so neither is read alone. That is the fourth time a key's placement or name has decided whether a rule exists.

FIFTH TIME. I wrote graphic_communications_out one version after v0.44 demonstrated that an ungated exclude reaches past its family, on a family whose boundary runs through graphic design. The pipeline caught it before it fired. The rule for this block, restated so it sticks: A FAMILY WHOSE BOUNDARY SITS NEXT TO AN INCLUDED FAMILY IS NEVER AN UNGATED EXCLUDE. It is a board, and artscan finds the next case.

override_register.count: Nine prefix overrides across 179 schools. Every one is a verdict the classifier got wrong on a clean sample — not a judgement call, not a preference, and in no case a contradiction of the content test. override_register.publication: Publish the full register — school, prefix, direction, the classifier's own verdict, the sampled titles, and the reason — as part of the methodology, not an appendix. An override a reader can check is a correction; an override a reader discovers is a thumb on the scale.
override_register.floor_not_ceiling:
The scan reads SAMPLED titles, so a prefix whose sample happened to miss its business courses would not appear. Five is a floor.

Converting it toward a ceiling costs nothing: for every prefix currently judged 'out', string-match the WHOLE prefix's titles — not a sample — for arts-business signal (entrepreneur, business, marketing, fundraising, arts administration, arts management, leadership). No API calls, no classification: it only decides which prefixes are worth a second look. Run it before publication.
override_register.string_scan_is_a_finder:
The whole-prefix string scan finds CANDIDATES. It does not decide them, and its hit ratio must not be used as the majority test.

The majority test exists to stop a HETEROGENEOUS prefix being admitted for a sliver: a 320-course music department with one Business of Music course. It does not transfer to a HOMOGENEOUS arts-administration prefix where the string match simply misses titles that carry no business vocabulary. SAIC's ARTSAD at 31 of 129 and The New School's NMGT at 25 of 119 look like minorities by ratio; the question is what the other 98 and 94 courses are. Arts policy, cultural theory and curatorial studies inside an arts-administration department are still that department. Music and theatre courses would not be.

So: read the non-matching titles before deciding. A ratio applied mechanically would have dropped SAIC's Artrepreneurship — at a top-ten art school — for the same reason a ratio applied loosely admitted 735 music courses at CalArts. Both are the same error: letting a count stand in for a reading.

SELF, 32 to 46. The INCLUDES list has said 'critique taught explicitly as a method' since v0.5 and the lexicon carried only `critical feedback`. PRACTICE, 33 to 55. 57 of 111 misses are internships and most of the rest portfolio courses; the lexicon had `portfolio review` but not `portfolio`, and nothing for placements. Recall 65.5%.

precedents.note: NOT RENDERED into any prompt. Rulings recorded so they are consistent across sessions and visible in the methodology. A precedent moves into the axis text only when the evidence shows the classifier is systematically getting that class wrong — which re-keys the axis cache corpus-wide and is never done for a single course.
precedents.producing:
PRODUCING IS VENTURE when the course teaches development, financing, packaging, rights and distribution — the producer raising money and assembling a project is building an enterprise around work. It is PRACTICE when it teaches operating inside a studio's apparatus as an employee.

UCLA FILMTV 287A and 287B are venture and the classifier applied the test correctly: 'development, production, and distribution... identifying material, attracting elements, and understanding basics of studio and independent financing and distribution.' Independent financing is the tell. No rubric change is needed for them.

287C is over-inclusion, and the analysis chat was right to separate it. Its subject is screenplay development for thesis projects — 'script analysis and creating set of viable development notes', 'completion of written outline' — with pitching as one element at the end. Primary subject is the student's own thesis project, which the rubric already excludes. It is ONE course in a three-course sequence with near-identical titles, and one course does not justify re-keying the corpus. Recorded, not acted on.
precedents.industry_as_scholarship: A course that teaches how a field operates, without the student transacting, is NEITHER axis — it is history and theory. 'The Art Market: Contemporary & Historical Perspectives' and 'Capital and Power in the Art World' are scholarship. So, probably, is NC State's 'Understanding the Arts Economies'. This is the branch that lets the venture figure stay low honestly rather than by timidity, and it is the one to watch in the 158.
precedents.watch_list: Marginal calls in the new evidence, recorded now so they are checked rather than rediscovered: SAIC 'Senior Seminar: Designed Objects Colloquium' reads as a capstone; NC State 'Understanding the Arts Economies' and 'Ecological Systems and Problem Solving in the Arts' read as scholarship. Three courses across two schools — noted, not ruled on.
precedents.half_b_ruling:
HALF B IS IN, and the binary is only tractable because Half A carves out the other side of it. Together the two halves implement the three-way test recorded in precedents.producing and precedents.industry_as_scholarship: transact on your own behalf is venture (Half B), study the field is neither (Half A), be prepared for employment is practice (already excluded).

Ruling Half B OUT would have removed UCLA FILMTV 287A and 287B, which v0.23 already found the classifier had judged correctly — 'understanding basics of studio AND INDEPENDENT financing and distribution' — and SAIC's Artrepreneurship, and NC State's EMA sequence. That is most of what the venture axis exists to find.

WHAT THIS RULING RESTS ON, stated plainly: the 158 disputed descriptions have still not been read. This is a DRAFT written to be tested by the gate, whose oracle was fixed before the run. If the gate's 21 expectations do not hold, the ruling changes before the $109 is spent, not after. No venture figure is published either way until the gate reports.
precedents.gate_1_failure:
The first gate spent $5.71 and failed 7 of 19. The diagnosis was the pipeline's and it was exact: THE INCLUDES WERE A LIST AND THE EXCLUDES WERE A QUESTION. A list matches lexically; a question needs the reader to hold two things at once. Sitting in parallel, the list won — so Coastal Carolina FILM 425 became venture on a sentence whose subject is 'Students examine the full spectrum of Hollywood's operations'.

Half A under-fired the mirror way: it named The Art Market and Understanding the Arts Economies as examples, and the two EMA courses that moved were the two whose titles matched those examples. Example-matching, not principle-application. So v0.31 names no example titles in the excludes at all — only the linguistic signals of analysis.

The fix is ORDER. Three questions, stop at the first yes, analysis first and employment second, so transaction vocabulary is never reached by a course that fails an earlier gate. The two controls that held under v0.30 — UT Austin RTF 347P and UNLV FILM 333 — held because they contain no transaction nouns; v0.31 has to hold them for the right reason instead.
precedents.287c_reversed:
FILMTV 287C's oracle expectation changes from [] to VENTURE, and it is a reversal of my own v0.23 read, made before the Half B wording existed.

Under the ordered test: not analysis; not employment — pitching your own thesis project to industry executives is seeking a greenlight for your own project, not applying for a job; and at question three the student is packaging and selling work they authored. That is venture. v0.23 called its subject screenplay development and excluded it as capstone — but the capstone exclude is about courses whose subject is MAKING the work, and 287C's subject is pitching it. The capstone line in v0.31 now says so explicitly.

Recorded as a reversal rather than folded into the other six failures, as the pipeline asked.
precedents.gate_2_failure:
v0.31 fixed every v0.30 failure and emptied the axis: NC State 11 venture courses to one, Western Carolina to zero, UCLA's producing sequence gone. $11.42 across two attempts, both the same mechanism in mirror image. v0.30's includes were a list of transaction nouns; v0.31's question one was a list of analysis verbs. A LIST MATCHES WHATEVER WORDS APPEAR, REGARDLESS OF WHAT THE SENTENCE IS ABOUT.

EMA 430 is the decisive case and the pipeline's read of it is the fix: 'Students analyze arts businesses through the use of case studies IN ADDITION TO EXECUTING AN ENTREPRENEURIAL PROJECT concerning the arts in a Raleigh community.' It says outright that it does both and names the analysis first, so stop-at-the-first-yes excluded a capstone in which students run a real venture. Almost every real arts-entrepreneurship course analyses something in service of building something, which makes any analytical component fatal under an ordered test.

So v0.32 drops the ordered stop-gates entirely. One pivot — equipped or informed — applied to the whole description, with analysis explicitly named as method rather than disqualification, and one disambiguation for whose venture it is. EMA 110 is the control that shows this is a balance and not a keyword: it contains 'students explore' and survived, because its subject is starting an arts business and nothing outweighs that.
precedents.adn_496: NC State ADN 496 'The Business of Art and Design' becomes an OBSERVATION, not an expectation. It went to practice under v0.31, caught by the employment question on 'the mechanics of gainfully applying their fine and applied arts education'. That phrase is genuinely ambiguous between making a living from your own work and being employed, and I do not have the full description. Rather than defend an expectation I cannot defend, it is observed and read after the run. Recorded explicitly as the pipeline asked, not folded into the other failures.
precedents.ucla_register:
UCLA FILMTV 287A and 287B failed v0.32 for their REGISTER: the catalogue opens with 'Introduction', 'Overview', 'understanding basics', and the pivot read that as informed. The students are first-year producers-programme students being equipped to produce their own films, and 287B has them presenting two unproduced screenplays toward their own thesis projects.

The pipeline's observation is exact and decides it: THIS IS THE SAME MOVE THAT FIXED EMA 430. That description names its analysis first and its execution second, and v0.32 correctly looked past the order. UCLA names its register first and its thesis work second. Treating one as presentation and the other as substance would be incoherent.

The addition keys on the student's own work being identifiable, which is what keeps the negative controls out: Coastal Carolina FILM 425 examines Hollywood's operations, RTF 347P explains how media industries operate, and in neither does a student make anything. Register was never what excluded them.
precedents.new_school_pair_practice: New School NFLM 0347 and 3473 move from an expectation of [] to an expectation of PRACTICE, recorded as a reversal. They went to practice under v0.32 and the classifier followed the disambiguation exactly: role-played Hollywood deal-making in hypothetical scenarios, on behalf of firms that are not the student's, described as business knowledge for people entering the film business. Practice is the better answer. The [] expectation was written when the only question was whether they were venture, and it predates the rule — the same shape of correction as 287C and ADN 496.

precedents.gate_3_failure:
v0.33 passed a 23-course board and stripped the axis's centre of mass. Measured against the disputed 158 — the venture-relevant population — it lost 27 venture verdicts and gained 9, net −18, while the art-unit total read +6% because gains elsewhere masked it.

how_to_compile: Each list has two kinds of term. An EXACT term matches only as a whole word: the pattern is \b + term + \b. A PREFIX term matches from a word start and may be followed by more letters: the pattern is \b + term, with no closing boundary. Matching is case-insensitive throughout.

The distinction is not cosmetic. 'artist' is EXACT in makers_practice, which is what stops it matching ARTISTIC. It is PREFIX in art_referent, where 'artistic' should count. The same string behaves differently in two lists on purpose, and that is the artefact fix of 2026-09-14 written into the rule.
In a multi-word term, a space matches a space or a hyphen, so 'start up' also matches 'start-up'. Terms are matched against the course TITLE only, never the description.

A ratio is the share of a prefix's distinct titles matching at least one term in that list. Denominator is the prefix's own titles, never the catalog. A prefix with fewer than 4 titles is not measured.
art_referent has one subtraction: a title whose only art-referent match is the term 'design', and which also matches a phrase in design_not_art, does not count. Nothing else is subtracted anywhere.

admin_only is computed, not listed: a title counts when it matches the admin list AND does NOT match makers_practice. A title naming both counts on the practice side. This measure is therefore asymmetric and leans generous toward any programme that puts entrepreneurship into an administration title — TCU ARLE reads 0.71 admin but 0.29 admin_only.

A term's meaning here is not its meaning in the axes. 'portfolio' and 'professional practice' sit in makers_practice because they ADDRESS a maker; in the axes they are PRACTICE and explicitly not venture. The maker rule decides who is in the art unit, never which axis a course carries. A reader who finds 'portfolio' in the rule that admitted an arts-entrepreneurship prefix should find this sentence before they find the apparent contradiction.

artefact_record: Two defects were found in the measure before it was published, both by rerunning it rather than by reading it.

'design' matched any sense of the word, including Career Design and Instructional Design. 1,524 titles in the corpus carry design in a plainly non-art sense. Fixing it moved eight prefixes below the art-referent line: Old Dominion IDT (0.54 -> 0.22), Cal State San Bernardino ETEC (0.50 -> 0.05), Cal State Fullerton IDT (0.75 -> 0.17), Kennesaw LDT (0.62 -> 0.38), Colorado State INTD (0.50 -> 0.47), George Mason EDIT (0.51 -> 0.49), UMass Dartmouth AED (0.50 -> 0.45), Utah State ISTU (0.50 -> 0.00).

It left SCAD ELDS at 0.93 — Electronic Design II, Visualization in Digital Design, BIM for Interior Design. That is the evidence the subtraction discriminates rather than blunts: a genuine design prefix keeps its score and the educational-technology prefixes lose theirs.

'artist' matched ARTISTIC, so East Tennessee FPAS (Artistic Vision I/II) read 0.60 on maker's practice and CalArts ICSE read 0.67. Word-bounding makers_practice drops them to 0.00 and 0.33. Both fall out of the rule. This is why the same string is EXACT in one list and PREFIX in the other.

A third artefact was found when the term lists were checked against the regexes the ruling was measured with, on 57,157 distinct sampled titles. The measured regex matched 'craft', 'film' and 'cinema' as bare substrings, so INTRODUCTION TO UNMANNED AIRCRAFT SYSTEM, SPACECRAFT AND SATELLITE ARCHITECTURE, Magic Witchcraft and Religion, and eleven Stagecraft courses all counted as art referents. Word-bounding removes them. 'start up' likewise matched Idea2Startup, and 'professional practice' matched Interprofessional Practice in Healthcare.

A fourth was found by the corpus check, not the sample check: the measured regex 'start[- ]?up' matched Startups as a substring, and the term list's exact 'startup' did not. Chapman ENTR read 0.50 on maker's practice and fell to 0.42 on one title, Managing and Scaling-Up Operations for Startups. 'startups' added. Chapman ENTR has art referent 0.00 and could never be admitted either way, so the rule's outcome never depended on it — but a term list that silently drops a plural is a defect whatever it happens to decide.

venture_definition.ruling:
BRINK'S RULING, 2026-09-15. It replaces Half A, Half B, the ordered test, the equipped/informed pivot, the register clause, the medium rule, the addressee clause and the employment branch with one distinction:

  DOES THE COURSE TEACH HOW TO MAKE JOBS, OR HOW TO GET ONE?

VENTURE: teaching entrepreneurship or entrepreneurial skills to art students, AT ANY LEVEL. Introductory, survey, theory, case study, ecosystem, economics of the field — you cannot run your own practice without first learning what one is, so the introductory and theoretical courses count. The enterprise need not be the student's own: manufacturer-level, community and social entrepreneurship, freelance and self-production all count.

NOT VENTURE: teaching how a broader marketplace operates. The Business of Hollywood, Business of Media, Business of Animation — describing studios, agents and industry structure is not teaching entrepreneurship.

NOT VENTURE: arts administration. It teaches people how to get a job, not how to make jobs. AADM, AMGT and ARTM stay unseated and the maker rule's outcome is unchanged, now with a plainer reason than CIP consistency.

SCOPE, NOT CLASSIFICATION: engineering entrepreneurship counts if it sits in the art unit and does not if engineering owns it. The art-unit filter already decides that and the venture axis says nothing about it.
venture_definition.what_it_reverses: HALF A IS REVERSED. EMA 365, 375, 520, 530 and 535 — arts economies, ecosystem models, entrepreneurship theory — are VENTURE under this rule. NC State returns to 11, which is where v0.29 had it before any of this began. Seven wordings were spent excluding courses this ruling restores.
venture_definition.shipped_text_predates_the_ruling:
STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT MATTERS FOR HOW THE AXIS IS READ: if the re-grade sends us back to v0.29, the classifier text in the rendered block PREDATES this ruling and was never written to implement it. The ruling is the axis's published definition; v0.29's text is the instruction that happens to implement it best, measured against a 158-course oracle re-marked to the ruling.

Its known defect is the marketplace branch — v0.29 admits industry surveys, which this ruling excludes. If the re-grade confirms that, the defect is published with the census: the courses are named, a reader can check each against the definition, and the disagreements are visible rather than buried in a rate. That is the whole argument for a census and it is why shipping an untuned wording is defensible here and would not be for a rank.
venture_definition.consequence_for_the_claim:
Brink's point, and it is the most important line in the ruling. '1.3% of art-unit coursework is building a creative enterprise' was computed under an instruction that excluded introductory and theoretical entrepreneurship. Counting those in RAISES the number and makes the finding harder to attack: art schools teach very little entrepreneurship OF ANY KIND, AT ANY LEVEL — which a dean cannot rebut by pointing at an intro course we did not count.

Every published venture figure computed before this ruling is superseded, including the ones in the analysis package. Recompute and reissue rather than annotate.

scope_questions.beyond_the_bottega_subjects:
Brink asks whether art education, art history and art theory should become categories of their own rather than exclusions, since the index already publishes practice, which is not a bottega virtue.

THE COMPOSITION PASS ALREADY DOES THIS, and the pipeline is right that adding axes would duplicate it at the cost of a new classifier, a new signature and a corpus re-run. Twelve exhaustive buckets summing to 100% produced the finding the whole project rests on: 73.4% of art-unit coursework is making and studying art — studio 46.1%, history and theory 27.4% — against 1.3% building an enterprise. History, theory and pedagogy are already counted, named and published. They are not axes because an axis asserts a comparison between schools and a bucket asserts a share of a curriculum, and these are shares.

One correction to the pipeline's framing: art education is NOT the missing bucket. `pedagogy` has been in the taxonomy since v0.6. What the exclusion changes is its scope, not its existence — see composition.pedagogy_after_the_exclusion.

RECOMPUTE COMPOSITION BEFORE PUBLISHING ANY OF ITS FIGURES. 1.3% predates the venture ruling and the corpus has grown; the composition signature has never moved, so it is free.

instrument_self_checks:
TWO GAPS FOUND ON 2026-09-16, both recorded because neither was anybody's assignment.

NOTHING AUDITS THE ART UNIT AT SCHOOLS WE ALREADY PUBLISH. gaps.py audits coverage against the roster; no equivalent asks whether the unit we drew is correct. UT Arlington is ranked on technology and practice with its 208-course ART prefix outside its art unit, and it was found by a fuzzy name match misfiring in an unrelated diagnostic. An art-unit audit belongs in the standing checks beside the integrity check, and it must run at every ranked school before any table ships.

A TITLE-BASED AUDIT ALWAYS OVER-FLAGS, and this is now a rule for reading any scan. The subject pass judges prefixes with programme context no lexicon can see: Colorado State's IDEA reads 0.88 art referent on titles like 'Design Your Life with Social Impact' and is housed in the College of Health and Human Sciences, not in art. The subject pass was right and the audit was wrong. A prefix appearing on a title scan is EVIDENCE IT IS WORTH READING, never evidence it is misjudged. The same caution runs in reverse: a scan that does not know about the maker rule flagged George Mason AMGT and Colorado State LEAP as defects when both are arts management, deliberately excluded.

THIRD GAP, and this one is mine. A subject-state change must be SCORED AND DIFFED AGAINST THE PUBLISHED RUN BEFORE IT BECOMES THE WORKING BASE. v0.43 became the base for three days of diagnosis without that step, and the diagnosis then attributed to stage 7 a defect stage 7 never had.

I RULED ON THAT ATTRIBUTION WITHOUT ASKING WHICH STATE WAS MEASURED. v0.44 said stage 7 could not ship because architecture sat inside RISD's and SAIC's art units; under the published subjects it did not, at RISD, SAIC ARCH, Penn, Oregon, Auburn, Kent, Hawaii, RPI or Tennessee. Stage 7's real architecture defect was three prefixes — Berkeley ENVDES, Boulder ENVD, SAIC AIADO. I blocked publication on a defect that did not exist in the published data, and the $24 re-roll followed from it.

THE QUESTION I SHOULD HAVE ASKED, and which now belongs on every diagnosis: IS THIS MEASURED AGAINST THE PUBLISHED RUN OR AGAINST THE WORKING BASE?

THE SUBJECT CLASSIFIER'S HELD-OUT TEST, 2026-09-21. On 75 institutions it had never seen, v0.46 admitted architecture or landscape into the art unit four times — Clemson LARC, Georgia LAND, Miami ARC, Rhode Island LAR — and excluded no design prefix. ONE DIRECTION ONLY. That is a characterisable bias, not noise: the v0.45 wording was written to stop the design over-removal and it succeeded, at the cost of under-removing architecture. The hand-applied board stays as a required step, stated in Methods §3 as a measured limitation of the classifier. A blind failure in one known direction, caught and corrected by a documented board, is a better result for the paper than a pass would have been — it is the negative result the review said reviewers look for and rarely see.

THE HELD-OUT CLAIM, CORRECTED 2026-09-22. v0.47 said the subject classifier failed blind in ONE direction only. That was wrong, and I wrote it. On 75 unseen schools and 7,919 prefixes it erred in BOTH directions: four built-environment admissions — Clemson LARC, UGA LAND, URI LAR, UAGM DSGN, all corrected by the board — and three in-scope exclusions at published schools, the largest ASU's 101-course art history department. Miami ARC was not a held-out school and leaves the count.

PUBLISH IT AS THE PIPELINE WORDED IT: 'on 75 unseen schools (7,919 prefixes) the subject classifier erred in both directions — four built-environment admissions, all corrected by the board, and three in-scope exclusions at published schools, the largest a 101-course art history department. The board and the pre-publication scans are required steps.'

The 'one direction' framing was attractive because a characterisable bias is a better story than noise. It was also a claim made on four rows without asking what the scan would find on the other side. That is the same shape as every title-read error in this project, made about the instrument instead of a course.

TWO OF MY OWN FILM-BOARD RULINGS FALL, and both for the same reason: I ruled on a column without reading the titles beside it. UCSC FMST was drafted as Film & Digital Media and I confirmed it; its samples read 'Advanced Topics in Feminist Theory'. Berkeley MEDIAS I admitted on its housing column, 'Film & Media', with 'Cultural History of Advertising' and 'Cybernetics and Cybercultures' on the same row — CIP 09, and CIP decides before housing is reached. My own film ruling says so. The pipeline disclosed its own draft errors on FI, FMST and MEDI first, which is how these two surfaced at all.

scope_gates.ruling:
GATE THE TWO INCLUDE RULES. Reversed from v0.41, which ruled pay $36.72 — the principle there was right and the cost-benefit was computed against a measurement that has since been retracted.

The pipeline reported 109 ranked schools affected and 88 moving 10% or more; its design regex was matching Machine Design, Structural Design and Reinforced Concrete Design, so the top of that list was civil and mechanical engineering, and it counted ARCH and LARC throughout. Same class as `craft` matching Aircraft. The real scope is the one in my own adjudication, because it came from reading titles: six design prefixes at 213 courses, eleven fashion prefixes at ~300, about 500 courses across fifteen schools.

At that size $36.72 is disproportionate, and Brink's rule decides it: the spend would be worth it if a large share of the published 144 were inaccurate, and they are not.

MY OBJECTION IS ANSWERED, NOT OVERRIDDEN. I ruled against gates because a gate can silently exclude the prefix a rule was written for — UCSB's film department was never asked. The pipeline's step 2 removes the silence: publish the list of every prefix the hints exclude and confirm DePaul DES, Minnesota DES and DESI, and Marist FASH are inside BEFORE anything runs. That is free, and it is exactly the check nobody ran when film's gate was written.
scope_gates.hints_must_be_published:
STANDING REQUIREMENT, whatever is decided about cost. If a rule only ever sees prefixes matching a keyword, THAT KEYWORD IS PART OF THE RULE and must be declared in the rubric beside the rule's text, never only in SHAPE_HINTS. A provost reproducing our method cannot see a gate that lives in code. film_media_in and art_education_out are currently gated on hints they acquired by accident — art_education_out picked up `education` because its prose happens to contain the word — and both should have those hints written into the rubric or removed.

AND NOW IT IS LOAD-BEARING. `design` and `fashion` are being added deliberately, so both must appear in the rubric beside their rules with the exclusion list they produce, not only in SHAPE_HINTS. Send the list from step 2 and I will write both into v0.43. Until then these two rules are published with a gate a reader cannot see, which is the condition I ruled against.
scope_gates.asymmetry_recorded: Two facts about run_classify_scope that are invisible from the rubric and shape every price and every reach. EXCLUDE rules have no shape gate at all — shape_matches applies only when direction is include — so every exclude asks all 1,308 art prefixes regardless of its subject, and museum_studies_out asks the same 1,301 questions as architecture_out. That is structural, cheap at $1.30 each, and good for correctness. INCLUDE rules are gated only if their text contains a SHAPE_HINTS key, of which there are exactly two, so an include rule with no shape asks all 18,356 out-prefixes. Both belong in the methodology, because a reader otherwise cannot tell why one rule cost nothing and another cost eighteen dollars.
scope_gates.pre_commitment:
STATED BEFORE THE RUN so an over-admission is visible rather than rationalised. design_schools_in and fashion_design_in each ask 18,356 prefixes with a majority test. I expect them to admit on the order of six to twenty prefixes between them — the six design prefixes and four fashion prefixes named in the adjudication, plus a tail. IF EITHER RETURNS MORE THAN FORTY, STOP AND READ BEFORE APPLYING. arts_business_under_education_in admitted 155 and its damage was only visible because someone read the list.

And the Minnesota housing check still stands: design_schools_in will ask Minnesota's DES, DESI and ADES and may admit them. Apply the housing check to its admissions BEFORE accepting them, per the IDEA principle — the rule cannot see which college a prefix sits in.
scope_gates.film_veto:
THIRTY PERCENT, and drop `dissertation` entirely rather than soften it.

The threshold is measured past its knee: 69 prefixes readmitted at 20%, 78 at 30%, 81 at 40%, 82 at 50%, flat above 30. UCSB FAMST — killed by a single `theatre` title among ten — gets asked. Binghamton THEA and Oregon JCOM stay vetoed on saturated samples, which is the veto doing its job.

The two-keyword rule stays exactly as it is. Lowering it to one would ask 891 prefixes and 48,666 courses including NYU LAW and Penn ENGL, which is a different instrument.

`dissertation` killed 34 prefixes including UCSB CH and Binghamton ENG. It is a graduate-catalogue word sitting in a list of family words and it has no business deciding whether a prefix is film. Remove it; do not weight it.
scope_gates.allow_new_followup: Approved for steps 1 through 4. The guard refusing follow-ups whose signature is not in the subject cache was built after makers_practice_in and has now done its job twice: it caught eight cold signatures and made $44.52 visible before it was spent, which is how the retracted measurement came to be checked at all.
scope_gates.gates_cost_discovery_not_coverage:
WHAT A GATE ACTUALLY COSTS, stated because 'the known-good prefixes survive' does not address it. A `design` hint finds prefixes with `design` in their titles. It will never find a design department named VIZ, MAKE, CRAFT or FORM. By construction the known-good list cannot test this, because those prefixes were found by a title scan using the same words.

So a gated rule codifies what we already found and automates it for schools arriving later — real value, and the reason these stay rules rather than reverting to the register the maker rule was built to retire. It does not discover.

THE ARTSCAN IS THE DISCOVERY INSTRUMENT AND IS NOW A STANDING CHECK. It scans every out-prefix by art-referent ratio rather than by rule keyword, it is free, and it is what found these prefixes in the first place. Re-run it whenever schools are added and whenever a scope family changes, and read its output as evidence worth reading rather than as a verdict. Gating the rules is only defensible because this check exists; if it lapses, the gates become the blind spot I objected to.

published_hints.note: These gates are part of the rules they gate and are published here, not only in SHAPE_HINTS. Both at need=1 with the 30% proportional veto. design_schools_in asks 3,688 prefixes and fashion_design_in asks 250, against 18,356 each ungated: $3.94 total, and all nine known-good prefixes pass.

`craft` MUST BE WORD-BOUNDED. published_hints.threshold_is_not_a_constant: The pipeline's point, and it belongs in the methodology rather than a code comment: film keeps TWO distinct keywords and design and fashion take ONE, because THE NUMBER IS A PROPERTY OF HOW COMMON A FAMILY'S VOCABULARY IS OUTSIDE THE FAMILY, not a constant to be applied evenly. Film, video and editing are common far outside film — lowering film to one would ask 891 prefixes and 48,666 courses. `design` and `fashion` are narrower words. Any future gate sets its own threshold on the same test and publishes the reasoning.
published_hints.blind_spot:
PUBLISHED because a gate's cost is what it never asks. 64 prefixes and 1,575 courses, 53 of them at ranked schools, are caught by neither hint.

DePaul DES sat at the top of that list at two keywords and drops out at one, which is the list doing its job — it is the instrument that made the threshold decision checkable rather than assumed.
